background.definition: DLE is a chronic form of cutaneous lupus characterized by photosensitivity, scarring, and skin atrophy. This condition is limited to the skin. Serologic abnormalities are rare.

list.listitem: The prevalence of SLE is 17 to 48 in 100,000.
The annual incidence of SLE in children is 0.8 in 100,000.
Approximately 20% of cases in a population-based series in Minnesota were DLE.
Fifteen percent of cases present in pregnancy.
The pathogenesis of DLE is not clearly understood. There is likely a genetic predisposition.
Up to 25% of patients with SLE will develop DLE. Discoid lesions account for 50% to 65% of cutaneous SLE manifestations.
Conversely, 5% to 10% of DLE patients will develop SLE. Such patients are more likely to have widespread discoid lupus with elevated ESR and elevated anti-single-stranded DNA antibody.
Ultraviolet light exposure or stress may activate a heat shock protein in keratinocytes, triggering gamma (delta) T-cell mediated epidermal cell cytotoxicity.

Skin biopsy may reveal any of the following: thickening of the basement membrane, follicular plugging, hyperkeratosis, atrophy of the epidermis, vacuolar alteration of the basal cell layer, lack of pigment, and lymphocytic cell infiltration in perivascular, periappendiceal, and subepidermal regions.
DLE is a clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic erythematous papule or plaque with follicular plugging, adherent scale, and atrophy. C
Skin biopsy can be used to aid diagnosis. C
Although patients with DLE usually do not have serologic abnormalities, serologic testing is recommended to rule out other autoimmune processes. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Patients often have symptoms/signs of systemic involvement, fulfilling diagnostic criteria of SLE
Plaques covered by silvery scales, symmetric and bilateral lesions, Auspitz sign, pruritic lesions
Erythema and telangiectasias, rhinophyma in extreme cases
Erythema nodosum, violaceous rash, lupus pernio of fingers and toes, systemic involvement
Painless lesions in sun-exposed areas, patients will typically give personal or family history of skin cancer
Chancre (painless ulcer), gumma with secondary bone pain
Flesh-colored or red papules that may coalesce, central involution, commonly affects hands and feet
Small lesions with rough texture, become red and scaly over time, sun-exposed areas

list.listitem: The primary lesion of DLE is characterized as scaly erythematous papules or plaques on sun-exposed areas, most often face, scalp, and neck. Lesions may also occur on upper torso and ears. Rash may be described as localized or widespread.

A systematic review of 29 studies found that white structureless areas (62%), arborizing vessels (58%), white scales (54%), and follicular keratotic plugs (47%) were the most common dermoscopic findings in scalp DLE. Follicular keratotic plugs (67%), white perifollicular halo (66%), white scale (39%), and speckled brown pigmentation (39%) were most common in non-scalp DLE.
Dilation of follicular openings occurs over time, leading to keratinous plugs.

As a lesion progresses, the overlying scale thickens and becomes adherent. The active border may become hyperpigmented, with hypopigmentation of central inactive area. Healing is marked by scarring and atrophy.
Lesions in the scalp may lead to scarring alopecia.
Patients may occasionally complain of pruritus and/or tenderness of discoid lesions, as well as arthralgias.

Initial laboratory studies should include CBC, UA, sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA, and anti-Smith antibody to evaluate for other autoimmune etiologies. If the diagnosis remains unclear, biopsy of lesion and normal skin should be obtained.

Unlike patients with systemic lupus erythematosus patients with DLE usually do not have serologic abnormalities. In patients with elevated single-stranded DNA antibodies there is a correlation between widespread DLE and an increased risk for SLE.

In a study of anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-ribonucleoprotein, specificity of these tests for diagnosis of DLE was much worse in a group of patients with other collagen vascular diseases than in a group of asymptomatic control patients.
A systematic review of trichoscopy found that follicular plugs and erythema encircling follicles were the most common findings in persons with discoid lupus erythematosus.
Suspect DLE in patients who present with characteristic lesions on sun-exposed areas. Take a careful history for pulmonary, renal, cardiac, and neurologic involvement.

Initial laboratory studies should include CBC, UA, sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA, and anti-Smith antibody to evaluate for other autoimmune etiologies. If diagnosis remains unclear, biopsy the lesion and normal skin.
Therapy is aimed at improving appearance and preventing scarring. C
Topical corticosteroids and systemic antimalarial treatments (eg, hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine) are the mainstays of treatment. B
The monoclonal antibody anifrolumab shows promise in several case series. C

The goal of treatment is to improve appearance and to limit scarring, which typically occurs in women. Treatment consists of systemic or topical steroids, or an antimalarial such as hydroxychloroquine.
Begin with a midpotency topical corticosteroid (eg, fluocinonide acetonide 0.05% cream) which will produce lesion clearing in approximately 25% of patients.
Limited research suggests hydroxychloroquine 400 to 1200 mg daily will produce clearing in approximately 50% of patients. Safety appears to be good with antimalarial treatment.
For patients with SLE with discoid lupus, systemic treatment with hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and methotrexate may effectively treat discoid lupus.

Anifrolumab is a monoclonal antibody titrating type 1 interferon receptor subunit 1 and has been approved for the treatment of systemic lupus. It was evaluated in a series of 10 patients with recalcitrant DLE. The CLASI-A disease activity score decreased by a mean of 65%, with 20% being the mean clinically important difference.
A series of 5 patients given tofacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, found moderate improvement in the CLASI activity score between 22% and 47% in 3 patients and no change in 2 others over 24 weeks.
A Cochrane review concluded that acitretin, a retinoid, is as effective as hydroxychloroquine.

An uncontrolled study of patients with discoid lupus refractory to antimalarials gave them acitretin 10 mg daily, increasing to 25 mg. Mean disease activity scores declined over 24 weeks with a marked response in 80% of patients.
These other immunosuppressants have been tried in uncontrolled studies: siolimus (rapamycin), efalizumab, topical tacrolimus, pimecrolimus, and thalidomide.
Lesion ablation—with carbon dioxide laser and argon laser—has been used, though clinical trials are lacking. Use of an argon laser has been reported to trigger cutaneous lupus.
A small trial (n=48) examined pulsed dye laser in patients with discoid lupus, and found some improvement in global assessment and texture in the treatment group.
Excision of scarred lesions may also be indicated for selected patients.
Encourage smoking cessation, since smoking may decrease the effectiveness of hydroxychloroquine or may worsen lesions.
Instruct patients to protect skin from sunlight by using sunscreen and protective clothing.
Approximately 5% to 10% of DLE patients will progress to SLE. B
Such patients are more likely to have widespread DLE with elevated sedimentation rate and elevated anti-single-stranded DNA antibody. B
